example: How much of the strip makes the three sides?
The joining tab overlaps; it is not a fourth side of the triangular stand.
exit: A revised stand uses two 3 1/4-in faces, a 4-in base and a 1/2-in joining tab. Find its blank length. Explain where you would measure the second fold from datum A. Cite your notebook and one test result.
key: Blank = 3 1/4 + 3 1/4 + 4 + 1/2 = 11 in. Second fold is 6 1/2 in from datum A. Actual tests vary; inspect independent tape use and a real revision, not only the digital answer.

example: Find the interior and outside width of three clear bays.
3 × 2 1/2 + 2 × 1/8 = 7 3/4 in interior; + 2 × 1/8 = 8 in outside.
Only the two internal partitions belong in the interior-width sum.
exit: Two clear bays each need 3 1/4 in. One internal partition is 1/8 in and two outer walls are each 1/8 in. Calculate outside width and identify the internal partition on your sketch.
key: Outside width = 6 1/2 + 3/8 = 6 7/8 in. Interior width = 6 5/8 in. Check that the student adds three thicknesses for the outside width, not two.

example: Can four rectangular pieces fit this sheet?
Each 4 × 3-in piece has 12 in² area; four use 48 in². Two rows of two fit in an 8 × 6-in rectangle.
A 9 × 12-in sheet can contain this arrangement. Area alone would not prove a different set of shapes fits.
exit: A 12 × 9-in sheet supplies six 4 × 3-in pieces. Show an arrangement, calculate used area and remaining area, and explain why the layout matters.
key: Three columns of 4 in and two rows of 3 in fit: 12 × 6 in. Used area 72 in²; sheet 108 in²; remaining 36 in². An equivalent rotated layout is acceptable.

example: Estimate the cost using classroom prices, not a supplier quote.
This is material consumed. Buying one whole sheet would cost $2.40 before tape or other supplies.
exit: Your build consumes 3/4 sheet at a classroom price of $2.40 per sheet and 4 ft of tape at $0.10/ft. Find consumed-material cost and the purchase cost if you must buy one sheet plus that tape.
key: Consumed cost = $1.80 + $0.40 = $2.20. Whole-sheet purchase = $2.40 + $0.40 = $2.80. Do not present sample prices as current quotations.

example: Check an inspected dimension.
Actual 8 1/8 in − intended 8 in = +1/8 in.
A teacher-set ±1/8-in tolerance includes both limits; whether this is suitable depends on the object and material.
exit: A plan calls for 6 3/4 in ±1/8 in. State the acceptable interval. Does an actual 6 7/8-in part meet it? Give your own final measurement and notebook reference.
key: Interval 6 5/8 through 6 7/8 in, inclusive. 6 7/8 in meets the stated dimensional tolerance. It still needs the functional fit test.

example: Find the center spacing.
Horizontal: 8 1/2 − 2 × 3/4 = 7 in. Vertical: 5 1/4 − 2 × 3/4 = 3 3/4 in.
Overall dimensions and center spacing are different quantities.
exit: If both horizontal edge offsets become 1 in while overall width stays 8 1/2 in, what is the new center spacing? Which two marks move?
key: Spacing = 6 1/2 in. Both left and right columns of centers move inward by 1/4 in; all four centers change horizontal position.

example: Compare improvement against a baseline.
Version 1 holds 4 identical objects; version 2 holds 7: (7 − 4)/4 × 100 = 75% more.
Object count is a comparative load measure, not force in newtons. A capped test gives a lower bound on capacity.
exit: A tower improves from 5 to 8 identical test objects. Find percent increase. Read the footprint limit from drawing D and explain why taller is not automatically stronger.
key: 60% increase. Footprint limit is 6 × 6 in. Strength depends on geometry, material, load path and stability; height alone is not evidence.

example: Calculate bearing from actual geometry.
A centered 11-in member over an 8-in gap has (11 − 8)/2 = 1 1/2 in bearing at each end.
The clear gap excludes the supports; total member length includes both bearings.
exit: A beam spans 9 1/4 in with 3/4 in bearing at each end. What minimum length is needed? Sketch where the three lengths sit.
key: 10 3/4 in. The three consecutive segments are bearing, clear gap, bearing. Material results depend on observed data.

example: Convert feet and inches consistently.
6 in is half a foot, not 0.6 ft.
exit: Convert a 9 ft 8-in surveyed length to inches. On drawing E, how far from the southwest corner is the far edge of the 3-ft door?
key: 116 in. Door far edge is 2 + 3 = 5 ft from the specified corner along the south wall.

example: Transfer real dimensions to the model.
16 ft × 1/2 in/ft = 8 in; 12 ft × 1/2 in/ft = 6 in; 3-ft door = 1 1/2 in.
Both plan and elevation must use the same chosen model scale.
exit: A 14-ft wall with an 8-ft height uses the model scale 1/2 in = 1 ft. Find model width and height. Explain what changes if a printed drawing is resized.
key: 7 × 4 in. Resizing changes the measurable paper scale; written dimensions remain the stated values. Verify a calibration dimension before scaling from paper.

example: Find a diagonal for a right-angled frame.
For a 6 × 8-in rectangle: d² = 6² + 8² = 100; d = 10 in.
This uses a right angle. Check the frame; do not apply it to an arbitrary four-sided shape.
exit: A right-angled bay is 3 × 4 in. Calculate its diagonal. Identify which view would show a brace on a vertical wall.
key: 5 in by the Pythagorean relationship. The wall elevation shows the vertical-wall brace; the floor plan alone does not show its height.

example: Estimate net covering area.
A 12 × 8-ft wall minus a 3 × 7-ft opening: 96 − 21 = 75 ft². With a stated 10% allowance: 82.5 ft².
Allowance is a planning choice, not a universal trade rule; purchase quantities depend on usable stock sizes.
exit: A 10 × 8-ft wall has a 2 × 3-ft opening. Find net area and area with a supplied 10% allowance. Identify the opening in the elevation.
key: 80 − 6 = 74 ft²; 74 × 1.10 = 81.4 ft². Do not subtract the opening perimeter from wall area.

example: Compare melting in a controlled test.
12 g melted from 60 g = 20%; 6 g from 60 g = 10%. Melt reduction = (12 − 6)/12 × 100 = 50%.
The enclosure halved melt in this trial; it did not establish a material R-value.
exit: A control melts 15 g and an insulated version melts 9 g in comparable trials. Find percent melt reduction. State one condition that must be held the same.
key: 40% reduction relative to control. Accept equal starting mass/temperature, duration, container, surroundings or handling. No R-value inference.

example: Calculate the effect of a measured change.
Deflection falls from 6 mm to 4 mm: (6 − 4)/6 × 100 ≈ 33.3% reduction.
Report measurement resolution; a small difference may not be meaningful enough to justify a strong claim.
exit: Movement changes from 8 mm to 5 mm. Calculate the reduction and name the baseline. Identify the revised feature on the relevant drawing view.
key: 37.5% reduction using 8 mm as baseline. A claim of improvement needs comparable actual testing and instrument resolution.

example: Convert a checked model dimension back to full size.
7 1/2 model inches ÷ (1/2 in per ft) = 15 ft.
The result describes the intended full-size dimension, not a physically validated full-size building.
exit: At 1/2 in = 1 ft, an opening measures 1 3/4 in in the model. What real width does it represent? Identify whether opening width is read from plan, elevation, or both when dimensioned.
key: 3 1/2 ft = 3 ft 6 in. Either dimensioned view can supply width; related views must agree.

example: Translate a revised opening offset.
At 1/2 in per ft, changing 2 ft to 3 ft moves the opening by 1/2 in in the model.
The designer must decide the intended offset before either view is corrected.
exit: A model door must move 1 ft 6 in at scale 1/2 in = 1 ft. Calculate model movement and list the drawing views that need checking.
key: 3/4 in. Check plan and the affected wall elevation, plus any detail or parts affected by the change.

example: Use an ideal displaced-volume model.
Equal piston areas predict equal travel: A × 20 mm = A × d, so d = 20 mm.
This model fits an ideal liquid system; trapped air, leaks and friction can change actual motion.
exit: For equal piston areas, predict output travel for 18 mm input in the ideal liquid model. State why an air-filled system may behave differently and identify input/output on G.
key: 18 mm ideal output. Air is compressible; water is much less compressible under this classroom condition. Real travel must still be measured.

example: Predict travel with a larger output piston.
A_in = 1 cm²; A_out = 2 cm²; input 4 cm: output = (1 × 4)/2 = 2 cm.
Ideal output force would double, but do not claim you measured a force ratio without force measurements.
exit: Input area 2 cm² moves 3 cm; output area is 3 cm². Predict output travel. Point to the mounting feature that prevents sideways motion.
key: Output = (2 × 3)/3 = 2 cm. An actual guide/brace must be identified; ideal force claims require the model’s limitations.

example: Calculate an average collection rate.
180 mL in 15 s = 12 mL/s. At that average rate, 240 mL would take 20 s.
A falling reservoir changes pressure head; the reported value is the trial’s average.
exit: A system collects 200 mL in 25 s. Find average flow rate and identify two conditions to hold constant when comparing a second tube.
key: 8 mL/s. Constant starting head, liquid, tube bore when not the changed variable, collection method and timing are valid choices.

example: Locate symmetric features from a centerline.
On a 3-in-wide hull, the centerline is 1 1/2 in from each edge. Pipes 1 in apart lie 1/2 in on each side of center.
Their centers lie 1 in and 2 in from the same edge.
exit: Two mounting centers must be 1 1/2 in apart, symmetric about the centerline of a 4-in-wide base. Find both locations from the left edge. Identify which drawing provides their spacing.
key: Centerline 2 in; offsets ±3/4 in; positions 1 1/4 and 2 3/4 in. A dimensioned plan/layout supplies spacing; schematic connectivity alone does not.

example: Check a simple liquid balance.
Start 200 mL; receiver 175 mL; liquid retained 20 mL: unaccounted volume = 5 mL.
Do not call all 25 mL missing from the receiver a leak.
exit: A 150-mL trial leaves 130 mL collected and 15 mL in the route. What volume is unaccounted for? Name one check needed before calling it a leak.
key: 5 mL. Check retained liquid, spills, measurement resolution and starting/ending conditions.

example: Calculate a boat’s average speed.
120 cm in 8 s = 15 cm/s.
Machine alternative: 6 complete cycles in 30 s = 0.20 cycles/s. These are different performance quantities.
exit: Choose your route: boat travels 150 cm in 10 s; machine completes 5 cycles in 25 s. Calculate its rate and name the drawing feature used to establish the measurement endpoints.
key: Boat 15 cm/s; machine 0.20 cycles/s. Accept the declared route only; endpoints must match its lane or completed-cycle definition.

example: Compare average performance.
Speed changes from 12 to 15 cm/s: (15 − 12)/12 × 100 = 25% increase.
For time over a fixed distance, a shorter time is better; label the metric before calculating percent change.
exit: A fixed task takes 20 s before revision and 16 s after. Find percent time reduction. Explain why that is not the same numerical value as percent rate increase.
key: Time reduction 20%. For the same task, rate rises by 20/16 − 1 = 25%. Each percentage has a different baseline quantity.

example: Check whether a test meets its stated requirement.
A gate must move at least 20 mm. Three trials of 22, 21 and 19 mm include one failure.
An average above 20 mm does not prove every trial meets an every-cycle requirement.
exit: A 20-mm minimum travel requirement gives trials 20, 23 and 18 mm. Does the machine meet an every-cycle requirement? Calculate the mean and explain its limitation.
key: No: the 18-mm trial fails. Mean = 61/3 ≈20.3 mm; averaging conceals the failed cycle.

example: Convert units before comparing readings.
2.4 cm = 24 mm; 24 − 20 = 4 mm above a 20-mm target.
Subtracting 2.4 from 20 without converting units gives a meaningless comparison.
exit: A drawing calls for 30 mm travel and you measure 2.7 cm. Find the shortfall and identify the start/end references to recheck.
key: 2.7 cm = 27 mm; shortfall 3 mm. Start and end must refer to the same moving point and reset position.

example: Estimate wire with a stated routing allowance.
A 14-in route plus 2 in for connections needs 16 in.
Allowance is stated for this kit and layout; it is not a universal wiring rule.
exit: Three routes are 8, 11 and 6 in. Each needs a supplied 2-in connection allowance. Calculate total wire. Identify the switch symbol in J.
key: 8+11+6+3×2 = 31 in. Switch interrupts or completes a path; merely drawing a line across it does not establish physical contact.

example: Calculate reliability from repeated trials.
Eight successful triggers in ten trials = 80%; ten in ten = 100% in that test.
Ten successes do not prove permanent reliability under all conditions.
exit: Nine of twelve trials succeed. Calculate success percentage. Explain why moving a symbol on a schematic need not mean moving the physical component.
key: 75%. A schematic represents connectivity; physical positions are given by the layout drawing.

example: Compare a reading with a nominal value.
A nominal 3.0-V source reads 2.8 V: difference = −0.2 V.
A nominal rating is not a guaranteed measurement; interpret readings with the circuit condition and instrument resolution.
exit: A nominal 4.5-V source reads 4.2 V. Find the difference. On the schematic identify two points for measuring lamp voltage and state the required measurement mode.
key: −0.3 V relative to nominal. Across the lamp terminals in the taught DC-voltage mode. Teacher verifies instrument-specific sockets/range.

example: Use Ohm’s law for an explicitly resistive example.
For a 30-ohm resistor at 3.0 V, I = V/R = 0.10 A = 100 mA.
Do not assume a motor, lamp or LED behaves like a constant resistor across all conditions.
exit: A supplied 60-ohm resistor is connected to 3.0 V. Calculate current in A and mA. Show where a current meter enters the series path.
key: 0.05 A = 50 mA. It replaces a break in the series path using the demonstrated setup, never bridges the source.

example: List every control state.
Two independent on/off switches give 2 × 2 = 4 states: off/off, on/off, off/on, on/on.
Testing only both-on does not establish independent control.
exit: List the four states and expected lamp outputs for two independent switches. If one 9-in route needs 2 in allowance, how long is that wire?
key: 00 neither; 10 first only; 01 second only; 11 both. Wire length 11 in. Match bit order to the labeled switch/lamp pair.

example: Calculate power for a supplied steady operating point.
A motor’s startup and changing-load behavior may differ from this steady example.
exit: A supplied steady device operates at 4.5 V and 0.10 A. Calculate power. Explain why that single value is not automatically its startup power.
key: 0.45 W. Startup/load conditions may change current; distinguish the supplied steady point from actual operation.

example: Calculate energy and sample operating cost.
Two 0.30-W lights for 4 h: 2 × 0.30 × 4 = 2.4 Wh = 0.0024 kWh. At a supplied $0.25/kWh, cost is $0.0006.
Sample electricity price is not a current tariff. Energy cost does not include battery purchase or equipment cost.
exit: A 0.6-W fan runs for 3 h. Find Wh and kWh. At a supplied $0.20/kWh, find energy cost and state one expense excluded.
key: 1.8 Wh = 0.0018 kWh; $0.00036. Excludes batteries, device purchase and other costs. Small model power legitimately gives a small energy-only amount.

example: Check a reliability claim.
Four required switch states × three repeats = 12 checks. Eleven passes means one condition still needs repair.
Do not hide a failed control state inside an overall average.
exit: Two switch states are tested three times each and one fails twice. How many checks passed? Explain what the failed state tells an inspector to investigate.
key: 6 total checks, 4 passed. Investigate the branch/trigger/connections associated with that state; percentage alone does not locate the fault.

example: Find an offset from a dimension chain.
Overall run 12 in; first segment 3 1/4 in; last segment 2 1/2 in: middle = 6 1/4 in.
All three lengths must refer to consecutive segments on the same route.
exit: A 15-in route contains 4 3/4-in and 3 1/2-in end segments. Find the middle segment and name the drawing needed to measure physical routing.
key: 6 3/4 in. Use the dimensioned physical layout; a schematic alone does not specify route lengths.

example: Explain a defensible performance comparison.
A task improves from 30 s to 24 s: time reduction = 6/30 × 100 = 20%.
Choose a metric meaningful to your product and preserve the original procedure.
exit: Using your own project, show a calculation with units and identify its baseline or reference. Interpret one supplied-plan feature and cite the notebook page containing its physical check.
key: Open response: verify operation, units, baseline/reference, drawing interpretation and actual check independently. Accept unsuccessful tests with a sound diagnosis; do not invent a numerical key.

example: Apply a stated dimensional tolerance.
Target 5 1/2 in ±1/8 in gives 5 3/8 through 5 5/8 in. An actual 5 3/4 in is 1/8 in above the upper limit.
Tolerance is a stated acceptance range; function still needs testing.
exit: A supplied part is 7 1/4 in ±1/8 in. State the interval and inspect a 7 3/8-in part. Then name one vocational skill you can now demonstrate independently, with evidence.
key: 7 1/8 through 7 3/8 in, inclusive; the part meets the dimensional interval. Individual evidence must support the student’s chosen skill.
